title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory evaluation to test whether embedding a formal reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent-to-configuration pipeline. Using a deterministic Dockerized emulator (FRRouting/Mininet-style topologies), two deterministic validators (containerized Batfish and a lightweight graph-based static reachability analyzer), and a matched sample of N=300 intents (150 benign operator intents and 150 programmatically derived adversarial variants), we compared single-pass generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline using gpt-5-mini under a preregistered protocol (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). Confirmatory analysis (paired McNemar-style test; 1,000–10,000 bootstrap resamples) found no difference: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability check on all 300 pairs (n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0), paired risk-difference = 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.0]. Exploratory diagnostics show no technical failures and deterministic accounting across 600 episodes and 300 model calls. We report the full preregistration, execution manifest, analysis artifacts, and limitations. The null result shows that in this controlled evaluation the selected baseline generation already avoided forbidden reachability under the chosen task set; this outcome highlights the need for harder, more adversarially effective, and production-representative benchmarks to evaluate GVR interventions for NetOps security.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency but raises safety concerns: LLMs can produce erroneous or security-relevant misconfigurations (reachability violations, accidental exposure). Prior system papers and surveys recommend integrating validators or closed-loop repair (generate–verify–repair, GVR) to improve correctness and compliance (e.g., verifier-guided IaC work and GVR-oriented code frameworks). Motivated by this operational concern, we asked: Does embedding a formal reachability/policy verifier in a GVR loop reduce the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent-to-configuration pipeline under a controlled paired evaluation? Our confirmatory contributions are: (1) a machine-readable preregistration (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specifying a paired N=300 design and prespecified analyses; (2) a deterministic Dockerized execution using FRRouting-style router images and two execution validators (Batfish and a lightweight static reachability analyzer); (3) open execution and analysis artifacts (600 episodes, 300 model calls) showing that, on this task set and model (gpt-5-mini), baseline single-pass generation already avoided forbidden reachability and the GVR pipeline produced identical outcomes (paired risk-difference = 0.0). We present design, confirmatory results, exploratory diagnostics, and operational implications.
sections.related_work: Recent literature establishes two empirical and architectural findings relevant to our design. First, generate–verify–repair and execution-guided iterative repair architectures improve correctness on code and IaC benchmarks when paired with strong verifiers or execution oracles (system papers on verifier-guided IaC and multi-agent repair frameworks). Second, surveys of LLMs in NetOps emphasize persistent risks—hallucination, overconfidence, and domain adaptation—that motivate verifier/validator integration and guarded generation. Work on TerraFormer and other IaC verifier-feedback systems demonstrates measurable gains on benchmark tasks; multi-agent self-correction and GVR loops (SAGE, AutoVerus-like systems) provide diagnostic signals that enable iterative repair. However, the literature also documents heterogeneity in gains across tasks, model sizes, and verifier strength and highlights gaps in execution-validated NetOps benchmarks that meaningfully stress security-relevant failure modes. Our study situates itself at the intersection of these findings by preregistering a paired verification experiment specifically targeting forbidden reachability as an operationally meaningful safety metric.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: We preregistered a deterministic paired experiment (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability), tested with a McNemar-style paired exact test (alpha=0.05) and 95% bootstrap CIs (1,000 resamples planned; 10,000 used in final analysis). Sampling: N=300 matched intent pairs (150 benign seeds, each with one adversarial programmatic variant) were generated deterministically; exact and fuzzy-duplicate removal rules were applied prior to execution. Intervention and baseline: For each intent pair we executed (A) baseline: single-pass LLM generation (one call to gpt-5-mini) and (B) guarded: LLM initial generation + verifier check + up to one LLM repair attempt (GVR loop), both executed against the same emulator topology and device profile in a paired fashion. Validators: containerized Batfish served as an execution-capable reachability oracle and a deterministic Python graph-based static reachability analyzer provided an independent check. Environment: All experiments ran in Docker compositions with FRRouting images and deterministic emulation; prompts, seeds, model settings, and orchestration code were frozen before execution. Outcome definition: 'Success' denotes absence of forbidden reachability as determined by the execution validators. Missingness and failure: Prespecified missingness rules treated technical failures separately and included sensitivity analyses; a single automated retry policy addressed transient API failures. Reproducibility: The preregistration, execution manifest, raw logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle referenced below.
sections.results: Execution summary: The run completed all planned episodes: 600 episodes (300 paired tasks × 2 conditions), 300 model calls consumed (initial shared-generation semantics resulted in one LLM call per pair), and zero failed episodes. Confirmatory (primary) outcome: complete_pair_count = 300; baseline_success_count = 300; guarded_success_count = 300; contingency table: n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples; seed 1729). Secondary estimands (preplanned) such as median_model_call_overhead_per_intent and verifier_disagreement_rate were recorded; model-call overhead distribution shows median overhead 0 given the shared-initial-generation design (detailed artifacts available). Verifier agreement: no disagreements observed in the recorded validator cross-tabulation for the recorded episodes. Representative per-intent artifacts and structured validator traces are provided in the archived manifest. Interpretation: Under the selected task generation, emulator, validators, and model, single-pass LLM generation already satisfied the forbidden-reachability constraint for every tested intent; embedding the verifier in a GVR loop produced no measurable reduction because the baseline already exhibited perfect compliance on this dataset.
sections.discussion: The null confirmatory result does not falsify the broader utility of GVR or verifier-guided repair in other NetOps contexts: prior work shows that verifier feedback can materially improve correctness on more challenging code/IaC tasks. Instead, our findings emphasize evaluation sensitivity: when baseline generation is already conservative or when task instances are insufficiently adversarial or trivial with respect to the safety predicate, a verifier insertion will by design show no incremental benefit. Operational implications: (1) evaluation benchmarks must include adversarially effective and production-representative failure modes to stress test GVR; (2) paired designs and preregistration help avoid post-hoc overclaiming; (3) researchers should report negative/null outcomes to refine benchmark difficulty. Limitations and open questions (below) detail external validity concerns—synthetic task generation, emulator vs production differences, single-model scope, and potential contamination—that constrain generalization. The study therefore argues for careful benchmark design (security-focused oracles, adversarial intent generation) before concluding on GVR effectiveness in live NetOps.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, deterministic paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent-to-configuration generation using gpt-5-mini across 300 paired intents. The confirmatory result: no difference between baseline single-pass generation and the guarded GVR pipeline on the forbidden-reachability safety metric (both arms passed on all pairs). This null result highlights the importance of benchmark difficulty and adversarial realism when evaluating GVR interventions for NetOps security. Future work should evaluate GVR pipelines on more adversarial, production-representative workloads, multiple LLMs, and under diverse verifier strengths to determine conditions under which verifier-in-the-loop architectures yield operational security gains.

limitations: External validity: tasks were synthetic and executed in Dockerized emulation (FRR-style), which may not capture production device heterogeneity or operational complexities.
Model scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; results do not imply multi-model generality.

Task difficulty and adversarial potency: the baseline generation exhibited perfect compliance on the selected task set; the result may reflect insufficiently adversarial or otherwise nonchallenging instances for the forbidden-reachability predicate.
Verifier scope: evaluation used Batfish and a lightweight static analyzer; other verifiers or dynamic execution oracles might produce different outcomes.

Contamination risk: deterministic duplicate and fuzzy-deduplication checks were applied, but residual training-data overlap with the hosted model cannot be entirely ruled out; sensitivity analyses are archived.
Secondary estimands were exploratory and provide limited inferential weight; no confirmatory benefit for model-call overhead or availability-regression was observed in the preregistered design.
